name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
description: A large-scale dataset for object detection and segmentation containing images of complex everyday scenes with common objects in their natural context. The dataset contains 91 object categories with 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization.
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
citeAs: T. Lin, M. Maire, S. Belongie, J. Hays, P. Perona, D. Ramanan, P. Dollár, and C. L. Zitnick,
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr using a novel pipeline that queries for pairs of objects in conjunction with scene-based queries to gather non-iconic images containing contextual relationships. The dataset harvested images containing multiple objects in natural environments rather than iconic, centered object views. Searches were performed for pairwise combinations of object categories (e.g., 'dog + car') and scene/object category pairs. At most 5 photos from a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. For categories where sufficient images could not be found, single category searches were performed with explicit filtering to remove iconic images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were sourced from Flickr, a photo-sharing platform containing photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: An explicit filtering stage was performed to remove iconic images for categories where sufficient non-iconic images could not be found through paired searches. Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed using detection methods, and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize near-duplicates across train/validation/test splits.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline consisted of three primary stages: (1) Category labeling: Workers indicated which object categories were present by dragging category icons onto one instance of each category. Eight workers labeled each image to ensure high recall. (2) Instance spotting: Workers placed crosses on all instances (up to 10) of each category found in the previous stage. The location of one instance from the previous stage was shown as priming. Eight workers labeled each image. (3) Instance segmentation: Workers segmented each object instance using a modified interface from the OpenSurfaces project. Workers were required to complete a training task for each object category before being allowed to segment instances. A single worker segmented each instance. (4) Verification: Multiple workers (3-5) judged each segmentation quality. Segmentations requiring at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were kept; others were discarded and re-segmented. For images with more than 10 instances of a category, remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single segment.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Worker quality was analyzed by comparing AMT workers to expert workers (co-authors). The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any individual expert worker. For category labeling, worker precision and recall were evaluated, showing most workers had high precision. Workers who completed the most jobs also had the highest precision. A leave-one-out evaluation procedure was used where a category was considered present if any of the remaining workers named it. For segmentation verification, each segmentation was shown to 3-5 annotators, with segmentations requiring at least 4 of 5 favorable votes to be accepted.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Category labeling: 8 workers per image. Instance spotting: 8 workers per image. Instance segmentation: 1 worker per instance. Segmentation verification: 3-5 workers per segmentation.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was split into two roughly equal parts. The first half (2014 release) contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The cumulative 2015 release will contain a total of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. The 2014 release is limited to a subset of 80 categories, with potential addition of segmentations for some omitted categories in the 2015 release.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses only on 'thing' categories (objects with clear boundaries) and does not include 'stuff' categories (materials and objects with no clear boundaries like sky, street, grass), though the authors note that 'stuff' categories could provide significant contextual information. The dataset is limited to entry-level categories rather than fine-grained categories to enable practical collection of significant instances per category. Some categories were removed from the 2014 release due to: too many instances (hat, shoe, eyeglasses), ambiguity and difficulty in labeling (mirror, window, door, street sign), confusion with other categories (plate with bowl, desk with dining table), or too few instances (blender, hair brush).
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for object detection and segmentation tasks. It addresses three core research problems: detecting non-iconic views of objects, contextual reasoning between objects, and precise 2D localization of objects. The dataset can be used for training and evaluating object detection models, instance segmentation models, and algorithms that require understanding of objects in natural contexts. Baseline performance analysis was provided using Deformable Parts Model (DPM) for both bounding box detection and segmentation tasks.
